strengths: Clear motivation backed by analysis: the paper identifies diversity collapse under reverse-KL on-policy distillation (§3.1: student retains 6.8% vs teacher's 18.5% high-entropy tokens) and illustrates instability of reverse-KL rewards with a controlled toy experiment (§3.2, Figure 1, Table 1), giving an interpretable account of why mode-seeking hurts in high-entropy regions.

The proposed method (EOPD, Eq. 9) is simple, principled, and well-integrated into standard PPO-style on-policy distillation; the top-k renormalized forward KL estimator (Eq. 10) with an explicit memory/probability-mass tradeoff analysis (Appendix F) shows practical care.

Broad empirical evaluation: three Qwen3 student scales, six math benchmarks (Avg@8 and Pass@8), out-of-domain benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AlpacaEval), Pass@k curves (up to k=128), a Llama-family replication (Appendix G), and useful ablations including the entropy threshold τ, forward KL placement (full/random), and comparisons against entropy-bonus and advantage-shaping baselines (Table 4) that show entropy preservation alone is insufficient.
The mechanistic evaluation (Figures 3–5, 11) connecting downstream gains to forward KL at high-entropy positions strengthens the causal story beyond benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea—mixing forward and reverse KL, selectively or adaptively—is close to existing work the paper itself cites (GKD's joint KL optimization, Wen et al. 2023's f-divergence minimization, TAID's interpolated distillation). The contribution is essentially an entropy-gated binary indicator over an already-known objective combination; a soft entropy weighting and comparison to divergence-mixing baselines like GKD variants beyond the 'full forward KL' proxy would better establish the delta.

The toy experiment's 'instability' finding may be partially artifactual: sampling is restricted to the student's top-10 indices (a hard capacity constraint absent in real LLMs), and top-1 change count conflates exploration with optimization instability; the mapping from this simplified setup to LLM training is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Statistical rigor is weak for the headline claims: the reported gains (+1.16 to +5.05 Avg@8/Pass@8) come from 8-sample estimates on small benchmark sets (e.g., AIME has 30 problems, so 1.25 points is a single problem); no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, and results are not uniformly positive (e.g., AIME25 for the 1.7B model: OPD 6.25 vs EOPD 5.83; AIME24 for the 4B model: OPD 18.33 vs EOPD 17.92; GRPO beats EOPD on MATH500-4B), suggesting some of the 'consistent improvements' may be within noise.

Table 6 weakens a central claim: full forward KL applied at all positions performs nearly on par with EOPD (e.g., AIME24 Pass@8 23.33 vs 23.33), so the benefit of selective placement over simply adding forward KL everywhere is marginal and not clearly distinguished from noise, undermining the 'selective placement is important' narrative.

Inconsistent thresholds across the paper (entropy ≥ 1.0 in §3.1/§5.4 vs τ = 0.8 in §5.5–5.6) make the diversity-preservation analysis and the objective gating not directly comparable; the interaction between the unclipped forward KL term and the PPO-clipped reverse KL term (e.g., double-counting gradient at high-entropy tokens, potential for oversized updates) is not analyzed.

No explicit limitations section, no code release statement, and the forward-KL top-k renormalization introduces an unquantified bias relative to the true forward KL objective that the theory prescribes.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly written. The observation that reverse KL causes diversity collapse in on-policy distillation (retaining only 6.8% of high-entropy tokens vs. 18.5% for the teacher) is a concrete, useful empirical finding.

The proposed method (EOPD) is simple and practical: applying forward KL only at high-entropy teacher tokens adds mode-covering pressure where the teacher is uncertain while keeping reverse KL's efficiency elsewhere. The design is cheap (top-k truncation of forward KL, ~15-20% of tokens affected).

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive for this line of work: three Qwen3 student scales, a Llama experiment in the appendix, six math benchmarks plus out-of-domain tests (GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AlpacaEval), Pass@k curves, comparison against entropy bonus and advantage shaping baselines, and ablations on the entropy threshold, forward KL placement, and top-k truncation.

The comparison in §5.5 is a genuinely informative control: entropy bonus matches EOPD's training entropy but not its forward KL at high-entropy positions, supporting the claim that preserving entropy alone is insufficient and teacher-anchored alignment matters.

The toy experiment (§3.2) and Figure 6 visualization isolate the instability of reverse-KL rewards under a high-entropy teacher in a controlled setting, and the appendix includes useful practical analysis (e.g., the top-k memory/probability-mass tradeoff).
weaknesses: The core method is technically quite incremental. Mixing forward and reverse KL, and weighting by teacher entropy, are both well-explored ideas (the paper itself notes the full forward KL variant is a form of GKD; alternative divergence objectives are cited in related work, e.g., Wen et al. 2023, Shing et al. 2025). The novelty reduces to a hard binary gate on the teacher's token entropy, and the paper does not clearly differentiate this from existing entropy-gated or interpolated divergence approaches.

The central 'instability' claim rests heavily on a toy experiment that is far removed from the actual setting (a single categorical distribution over V=80, no autoregressive conditioning, top-10 capacity restriction). The connection between this toy instability and the LLM training dynamics is asserted rather than demonstrated; the LLM-side evidence (Figures 5 and 11) is consistent but correlational.

Reported gains are modest and fragile. The headline improvements (+1.16/+0.99/+1.80 Avg@8) come with no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite evaluation on very small test sets (AIME has 30 questions, so a Pass@8 difference of 23.33 vs 20.00 is a single question). On several benchmark/metric combinations EOPD actually underperforms OPD (e.g., AIME25 Avg@8 for the 1.7B model, Minerva and OlympiadBench Avg@8 for the 4B model, AlpacaEval WR), and on Llama EOPD is 'competitive' rather than clearly better. The robustness of the improvement is not established.

There is an unexplained inconsistency in the experimental setup: the 0.6B and 1.7B students are trained on MATH while the 4B student is trained on a different dataset (DAPO-Math-14k), making cross-scale comparisons of the method's effectiveness hard to interpret, and the reason for this choice is not justified.

The paper contains no explicit limitations section. Given that the method introduces a new hyperparameter (τ), a temperature-sensitive entropy threshold that interacts with the teacher's logit scale, and a top-k truncation of forward KL, a candid discussion of when the approach would fail (e.g., low-entropy teachers, students much smaller than 0.6B, domains without verifiable answers) would be appropriate.

No code release or statement of artifact availability is mentioned, and some details needed for exact reproduction (e.g., number of training steps, compute budget, verl configuration specifics beyond Table 8) are incomplete.

strengths: The paper identifies a well-motivated and clearly articulated limitation of reverse-KL-based on-policy distillation (diversity collapse and unstable learning signals at high-entropy teacher positions), and the diagnosis is supported by three complementary pieces of evidence: a token-level entropy analysis (§3.1), a controlled toy experiment isolating the objective from LLM complexity (§3.2), and training-dynamics measurements of forward KL at high-entropy positions (Figures 5 and 11).

The proposed EOPD method is simple, well-integrated into standard PPO-style OPD pipelines, and the entropy-gated forward KL is applied to only ~15-20% of tokens, so the claimed efficiency retention of on-policy training is plausible.

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive: three Qwen3 student scales (0.6B/1.7B/4B), six math benchmarks, out-of-domain general reasoning and instruction-following evaluations, Pass@k curves showing the gap widens with k, a Llama-family replication in Appendix G, and useful ablations on the threshold τ, forward-KL placement (full/random), and top-k truncation tradeoffs (Appendix F).

The comparison against entropy-driven baselines (entropy bonus, advantage shaping) in §5.5 is a good experimental design choice, showing that entropy preservation alone does not explain the gains and that teacher alignment in high-entropy regions is the relevant factor.
Hyperparameters, chat templates, and evaluation protocols are documented in detail in the appendices, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is insufficient. Benchmark gains are modest (Avg@8 +0.99 to +1.80 over OPD), yet no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the main results, despite small evaluation sets (AIME24/25 have only 30 problems each; 8 samples per question). Several per-benchmark differences in Table 2 are within plausible sampling noise, and no multi-seed training runs are reported for the LLM experiments.

The toy experiment (§3.2) largely confirms well-known theoretical properties of reverse KL (mode-seeking behavior and high-variance gradients for heavy-tailed targets, e.g., Minka 2005, which the paper itself cites). The contribution of this experiment is limited, and the jump from a V=80 categorical toy setting to LLM-scale claims about 'unstable learning signals' is only indirectly supported by the forward-KL trajectories.

Novelty is modest. Entropy-gated mixing of forward and reverse KL is a fairly straightforward combination of standard components, and the paper itself notes the full forward-KL variant is close to GKD. Table 6 shows the 'Full' forward-KL baseline is competitive with EOPD on most benchmarks, weakening the claim that entropy-aware placement is decisively important; the AIME24 advantage (10.42 vs 8.75) rests on very few problems.

The instability analysis at LLM scale is somewhat circular: forward KL at high-entropy positions is measured on a student trained with reverse KL, and reverse KL is not designed to minimize forward KL, so high forward KL there is expected and does not by itself establish 'unstable' or non-convergent training signals.

Computational overhead of EOPD relative to OPD (extra teacher entropy and top-k queries, memory in Appendix F) is discussed qualitatively but never compared against OPD/GRPO wall-clock or memory in the main results, making the 'efficiency retained' claim hard to verify.

Mixed model configurations raise concerns: Base-model students are trained with an Instruct-style chat template in some settings and Base templates in others (Appendix A), and the KD/GRPO baselines use different rollouts-per-prompt; it is not fully clear all baselines were tuned comparably, e.g., the learning rate and epochs for GRPO.

There is no explicit limitations section, and some claims in the abstract ('yields unstable learning signals', 'essential for maintaining diversity') are stronger than the evidence, which is correlational; the paper itself labels the mechanism as a hypothesis in §5.4.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a concrete limitation of reverse-KL-based on-policy distillation (diversity collapse and unstable learning signals at high-entropy teacher tokens) and provides both a motivating token-level entropy analysis (6.8% vs 18.5% high-entropy token retention) and a controlled toy experiment to support the mechanism.

The proposed EOPD method is simple, principled (mode-seeking vs mode-covering complementarity), and cheap: it reuses teacher forward passes already needed by OPD, with measured overhead of ~4.5% per training step and 7.37x memory savings versus full forward KL.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three Qwen3 student scales, an additional Llama-3.2 family experiment, six math benchmarks plus out-of-domain evaluation, Pass@k curves up to k=128, and comparisons against strong and recent baselines (KD, GRPO, OPD, GKD with tuned lambda, entropy bonus, advantage shaping, BD-KD, AKL, ToDi).

Ablations are thorough and support design choices: entropy threshold tau, forward KL coefficient alpha, top-k truncation, forward-KL placement (full/random/entropy-gated), and diagnostic analyses (training entropy dynamics and forward KL at high-entropy positions) that go beyond just benchmark scores.
Good reproducibility support: implementation on standard frameworks (verl, DistillKit), full hyperparameter tables, chat templates, evaluation prompts, and computational cost breakdowns are provided.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: entropy- or discrepancy-gated selection between divergence objectives already exists (TODI, BD-KD, AKL are compared as baselines, and the related work admits this). EOPD is essentially a teacher-entropy-gated switch of forward KL on top of standard OPD, so the contribution is an incremental variant of a well-known idea.

Statistical rigor is insufficient for the magnitude of the claims: main benchmark results are single runs with no error bars or significance tests, while several reported gains are small (e.g., +1.16 Avg@8 for 0.6B) and AIME24/25 have only 30 problems each, making differences of 1-2 points well within plausible noise.

The toy experiment (categorical distribution, top-10 capacity-limited student, fixed multi-modal teacher) is quite stylized; 'instability' is characterized via top-1/top-10 change counts, and the gap between this toy evidence and actual LLM training dynamics is not formally bridged.

Results are mixed in places, which the paper downplays: e.g., GRPO outperforms EOPD on Minerva Avg@8 and several 4B rows, KD/GRPO beat EOPD on some AIME25 entries, and AlpacaEval win rate slightly favors OPD; the narrative of 'consistent improvements' overstates the evidence somewhat.

Hyperparameters (tau=0.8, alpha=1.0, k=16) are tuned on the same 1.7B/benchmark setup used for headline comparisons, and no held-out tuning protocol is described; the absolute entropy threshold tau=0.8 is teacher-specific, raising transferability questions.
The claimed URL for public code is empty in the abstract, which weakens reproducibility as submitted.

The top-k renormalized forward KL approximation (Eq. 10) changes the effective objective; while ablated, there is no analysis of bias introduced by renormalization versus true forward KL, particularly at genuinely high-entropy positions where the top-16 mass may be spread thin.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical problem: mode-seeking behavior of reverse KL in on-policy distillation, which is becoming a standard post-training recipe. The motivation that high-entropy teacher tokens encode meaningful reasoning-path uncertainty is well grounded in recent literature (Wang et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025).

The empirical evaluation is broad: three Qwen3 student sizes, a Llama-3.2-3B student, six math benchmarks plus out-of-domain evaluation, Pass@k curves, and many ablations (threshold τ, coefficient α, top-k, forward-KL placement). The comparisons cover KD, GRPO, OPD, GKD, entropy-driven baselines, and adaptive-KL baselines (BD-KD, AKL, ToDi), which is more thorough than typical.

The toy experiment (§3.2) and the token-level entropy analysis (§3.1, §5.4) give intuitive support for the failure mode being addressed, and the analysis in §5.5 (showing entropy bonuses raise entropy but do not align the student with the teacher in uncertain regions) is an insightful diagnostic.

Reproducibility treatment is decent: hyperparameter tables, chat templates, computational overhead analysis (4.5% step-time overhead, memory costs), and a top-k probability-mass/memory tradeoff analysis are provided.
weaknesses: The central method is a simple heuristic: gate an additional forward-KL term on teacher entropy exceeding a fixed threshold (Eq. 9). Entropy- or discrepancy-weighted combinations of forward/reverse KL already exist (the paper itself compares to BD-KD, AKL, ToDi, which do essentially this at token level). The novelty over these adaptive-divergence methods applied in an on-policy setting is modest.

Claims of 'consistent improvements' are overstated relative to the evidence. In Table 2, EOPD loses to OPD on several cells (e.g., Qwen3-4B AIME24 Avg@8 17.92 vs 18.33; Minerva Avg@8 39.71 vs 40.08) and to GRPO elsewhere, and the margins on AIME24/25 (30 problems each) are far within plausible sampling noise. No error bars, standard deviations, or significance tests are reported for any main result.

The 'instability' claim motivating the method rests on a heavily simplified toy setup (categorical distributions, no autoregressive conditioning, and an artificial top-10 capacity restriction on the student). This top-10 truncation itself plausibly causes the observed non-convergence, so the causal link between teacher entropy, reverse-KL gradients, and instability in real LLM training is not firmly established.

There is an internal tension in the method: forward KL is applied exactly at high-entropy positions, yet it is approximated over only the teacher's top-16 renormalized tokens (Eq. 10). At high-entropy positions, top-16 cumulative mass is lowest (the saturation in Fig. 10 is aggregated, not conditioned on entropy), so the forward-KL signal at the positions the method targets may be most distorted by truncation. This is not analyzed.

The experimental setup is inconsistent across scales: the 0.6B/1.7B students train on MATH while the 4B student trains on DAPO-Math-14k, making cross-scale comparisons of the reported gains (+1.37 → +5.05) hard to interpret. Llama results are also weaker and mixed (GRPO beats EOPD on MATH500 Avg@8).
The code link in the abstract is blank ('publicly available at' with no URL), which undermines the reproducibility claim as submitted.

The theoretical framing is thin: there is no analysis of the bias introduced by adding forward-KL to the clipped reverse-KL surrogate, of the interaction between α and the PPO clipping, or of when a hard entropy threshold should outperform a continuous weighting.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and well-motivated problem: reverse-KL on-policy distillation causes diversity collapse and unstable gradients at high-entropy teacher tokens, supported by both a token-level entropy analysis (6.8% vs 18.5% high-entropy tokens retained) and a controlled toy experiment (§3.2).

The proposed EOPD method is simple, well-specified (Algorithm 1, Eq. 9-10), and cheap: the paper quantifies the overhead (~4.5% per training step, ~7.4x memory saving vs full forward KL), which strengthens the practical claim of retaining OPD efficiency.

The empirical evaluation is broad and reasonably thorough: three Qwen3 student scales, a Llama family replication (Appendix G), out-of-domain evaluation (§5.3), comparisons against KD, GRPO, GKD, entropy-bonus/advantage-shaping baselines (§5.5), adaptive-KL baselines BD-KD/AKL/ToDi (Appendix H), and ablations over τ, α, and top-k (Appendix I).

The mechanistic analyses (Figures 3-5, 9-11) are a highlight: they go beyond benchmark numbers to show that EOPD better preserves high-entropy probability mass and achieves lower forward KL at high-entropy positions, directly supporting the paper's hypothesis about uncertainty transfer.
The writing is generally clear, the related work is well positioned, and the code is stated to be publicly available, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is insufficient for the headline claims. Several benchmarks (AIME24/25) contain only ~30 problems, and Pass@8 differences of a few points (e.g., 6.25 vs 8.83 for AIME25, 1.7B) are likely within sampling noise. No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported for the main results (only the toy experiment uses 3 seeds).

The toy experiment (§3.2) has a confound: Scenario A uses temperature 0.3 and Scenario B uses temperature 1.0 (Table 1), so the observed instability in top-1/top-10 dynamics could partly reflect temperature-driven sampling noise rather than teacher entropy per se. A temperature-matched control is needed to isolate the effect.

The forward KL term is an expectation over the teacher distribution, but it is evaluated on student-sampled tokens with a top-k renormalized teacher (Eq. 10). This is a biased, off-distribution estimate of forward KL, and the paper does not analyze the bias or its consequences; a theoretical or empirical treatment of this mismatch would strengthen the methodology.

Novelty is modest. Adaptively mixing or routing KL objectives based on teacher/student entropy or distribution mismatch is an active line of work (BD-KD, AKL, ToDi, TADI, generalized JSD-based approaches are all cited); EOPD's specific entropy-threshold routing is a reasonable but incremental variant, and the advantage over these baselines, while consistent, is not dramatic.

The ablations are conducted only on the Qwen3-1.7B student; it is unclear whether τ=0.8, α=1.0, k=16 transfer across model scales, and the τ=0.8 setting coincides with the best ablation result, raising mild tuning-concerns for the reported gains.

The causal link between preserved high-entropy mass and downstream accuracy is asserted rather than established: Figure 3/5 show EOPD tracks the teacher better, but no experiment (e.g., correlating entropy preservation with per-benchmark gains, or intervening on entropy preservation) directly demonstrates that this mechanism drives the benchmark improvements.
